channel.title: Deseret News - Faith
channel.description: Faith news and stories from Deseret News

item.title: How President Dallin H. Oaks is leading Latter-day Saints through a ‘glorious season of temple building’
item.description: Nearly a year after President Dallin H. Oaks was ordained on Oct. 14, 2025, Deseret News finds his tenure defined less by new temple announcements, which he deliberately slowed, than by faster progress on the 163 temples already in the pipeline out of the church's 385 total. Thirteen temples have been dedicated in his first year, two of them by Oaks himself in Burley, Idaho, and Belo Horizonte, Brazil, and 2026 is on track to rank second only to 2000, when 34 were dedicated. The First Presidency has also shifted announcements to local leaders, naming new temples in Portland, Maine; Marysville, Washington; and Otavalo, Ecuador. The dedications in Harare, Zimbabwe, and Alabang, Philippines, completed the last temples announced under President Thomas S. Monson, and the article closes with a status list for every temple still under way as of Oct. 1.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ donates over $7 million to American Red Cross
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is giving the American Red Cross more than $7 million for blood collection and disaster response, along with $850,000 for western Pacific communities hit by Super Typhoon Sinlaku in April. Bishop W. Christopher Waddell of the Presiding Bishopric framed the gift as caring for neighbors, Red Cross CEO Cliff Holtz praised the church's long partnership, and Utah/Nevada regional CEO Heidi Ruster said a Murray investment will expand capacity in the state. The relationship traces back to correspondence between Clara Barton and Relief Society leader Emmeline B. Wells in the 1890s, and since its first blood drive in 1996 the church has become the single largest contributor to Red Cross drives. Previous gifts totaled $5.1 million last year and $7.35 million in 2024, and the church reported $1.58 billion in welfare and humanitarian spending in 2025.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Can fighters be peacemakers? Inside the minds of Christians in MMA
item.description: With the UFC holding 14 fights at Salt Lake City's Delta Center on Saturday, Oct. 3, while Latter-day Saints meet a few blocks away for general conference, Deseret News asked whether cage fighting fits with Christian discipleship and peacemaking. The piece notes a wave of on-air faith declarations in 2026, including middleweight Bo Nickal quoting scripture at a White House card watched by 34 million, Mauricio Ruffy urging viewers to give their lives to Jesus, and Jalin Turner telling a UFC 330 crowd that a revival is under way. Podcaster and amateur fighter Cade Alvey argued that fighting and peacemaking rarely collide and that MMA gyms can be friendlier than rec-league softball. Pro and local fighters interviewed described treating bouts as sport rather than hatred, using the microphone to share their faith, and finding that the suffering of training draws them closer to Christ, with one comparing restrained force to the Book of Mormon account of Ammon.
item.dc:creator: Krysyan Edler and Aaron Shill

item.title: A tale of 2 temples: The reconstruction and slight relocation of the Anchorage Alaska Temple
item.description: For roughly the next five months, the two closest temples of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints are both in Anchorage, Alaska: the original Anchorage Alaska Temple and its replacement, being built about 80 yards away. That gap beats the long-standing record holders in Utah, where the Provo City Center and Provo Utah Rock Canyon temples have sat about 2.3 miles apart since 2014. The Church News piece examines the rebuild and small move of the Alaska temple. Deseret News runs only a brief excerpt, and the full story is on TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ names new Area Seventy in leadership meeting
item.description: Elder David Kannar, 64, of Queensland, Australia, was sustained as a new Area Seventy during the leadership meeting held Thursday ahead of the October 2026 general conference of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. He will serve in the Eighth Quorum of the Seventy, which covers the Pacific and Philippines areas, replacing Elder Robert H. Simpson, who had served since April 2021. Kannar and his wife, Sally-Jane, have four children and previously led the Cameroon Yaoundé Mission. Area Seventies, called by the First Presidency, typically serve part-time for about five years while keeping their regular jobs.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: How the Church turned competition into collaboration for 8 global humanitarian organizations
item.description: Faced with humanitarian groups that often compete with each other for donors, government aid and volunteers, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has paired eight of them into four consortia that share the work. The arrangement is part of the Caring for Women and Children Initiative, which the church expanded in 2024 and which targets 12 high-need countries such as Nepal, Nigeria and Kenya. One group of three partners concentrates on nutrition and medicine, supplying supplements, vitamins and more nourishing food. The Church News report is a short preview, and the full article is posted on TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Keith McMullin, former CEO of Deseret Management, dies at age 85
item.description: Keith B. McMullin, former member of the Presiding Bishopric of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and CEO of Deseret Management Corp. from 2012 to 2023, died Wednesday at age 85. H. David Burton, who served alongside him in the bishopric for nearly 20 years, described a leader who weighed every decision by its effect on people, and DMC executives Sheri Dew and Gary Porter recalled him as a gracious boss and wise mentor. Born in St. George in 1941, McMullin studied finance at the University of Utah, worked at Ford Motor Co. and spent two decades in church welfare services before his 1995 bishopric call. He saw his business career as part of his faith, and he was honored with two Utah business awards in 2024.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Institute celebrates its 100th anniversary on the date and at the place where it all began
item.description: Moscow, Idaho, home of the University of Idaho, is where the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' Institutes of Religion program began a century ago, and it is also where the centennial was marked. Church President Heber J. Grant sent J. Wyley Sessions there on Sept. 26, 1926, to start "collegiate seminaries," with no building or curriculum and an initial class of 25 students. The Deseret News page is a brief excerpt, and Church News has the full report on the commemoration.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Why we all need more rituals
item.description: In this State of Faith newsletter essay, Mariya Manzhos describes a workshop at the Restore conference led by Casper ter Kuile, author of "The Power of Ritual" and former co-host of the podcast "Harry Potter and the Sacred Text." Ter Kuile, who is not religious, said rituals give people "a home in time," and he distinguished a ritual from a routine by its intention and meaning, adding that even a skin-care routine can work as a memento mori. Participants traded inventive family traditions and drew up a yearly ritual calendar, which led Manzhos, who grew up with few family traditions, to conclude that her life already had enough rituals but lacked deliberate preparation and a story behind them. The newsletter also looks at why heavily secular France gave Pope Leo XIV a huge welcome, noting that only 8% of French adults attend church.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: Former NYT columnist makes a case for God and religion
item.description: Ross Douthat, a Catholic writer who spent 17 years as a New York Times columnist and now reports for "60 Minutes," told a BYU forum audience Tuesday that everyone should be religious. He finally made it after a February snowstorm and a second weather threat had delayed his visit, and joked that either dark powers or God was sending him a message. Douthat said no single argument proves God exists, but several lines of evidence together make belief reasonable: physical constants finely tuned for life, the mystery of human consciousness, and spiritual experience that has persisted even as institutional religion has weakened. He urged believers to live their faith with confidence rather than embarrassment, and he develops the case further in his book "Believe: Why Everyone Should Be Religious."
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Temple Square is transforming. Here’s what you can see right now
item.description: With the Salt Lake Temple nearing the end of a renovation of almost seven years, the Deseret News outlines which parts of Temple Square visitors can see now and which remain closed. The temple itself is still closed, but the surrounding gates and walkways have reopened, so visitors can get close to its 19th-century exterior; Welfare Square and the new Humanitarian Center nearby are also open for tours. The Conference Center will reopen briefly for general conference on Oct. 3-4 and a few other events before closing again through March 1, 2027. Public temple tours will run April 5 through Oct. 1 next year, and the next batch of tickets opens Oct. 1 at 6 p.m. MDT.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Latter-day Saints share honors for interfaith efforts and charity at Boston Red Sox game
item.description: Members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in Boston gathered at Fenway Park on Wednesday, Sept. 23, for a Latter-day Saint Night that doubled as a recognition of local community and interfaith work. The Red Sox beat the Cleveland Guardians 1-0 that evening. Four honorees were recognized on the field before the game: Matthew Christensen, who previously led the Cambridge Massachusetts Stake; the Rev. Mark Scott, associate pastor of the Azusa Christian Community; Pastor Reba Danastorg of Imani Temple Church of God in Christ; and Dr. Gordon Williams, a Harvard medical professor and Latter-day Saint. Church News, which reported the event, directs readers to TheChurchNews.com for its full account.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ advances first international temple announced under President Oaks
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has settled on a site for the Otavalo Ecuador Temple, the first international temple announced under church President Dallin H. Oaks and the first of his three announced temples to have a site map released. The First Presidency said the temple will occupy a 6.05-acre parcel on the outskirts of Otavalo in northern Ecuador and will run roughly 18,850 square feet. The temple was announced less than six months ago, on May 14, during a devotional for local members, with the First Presidency calling it a reason to rejoice and a blessing that would give members more frequent access to temple ordinances and covenants. The Portland Maine and Marysville Washington temples, also announced under President Oaks, remain in planning and design. The First Presidency separately announced that groundbreaking for the Cuernavaca Mexico Temple — one of 27 in that country — will be held Saturday, Nov. 14, presided over by Elder Moises Villanueva, president of the church's Mexico Area.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: A year after the Grand Blanc church shooting, survivors cling to faith as memory haunts them
item.description: A year after a man drove a pickup into the front wall of a Latter-day Saint chapel in Grand Blanc, Michigan, and opened fire on 215 worshippers, survivors told the Deseret News that recovery has been neither quick nor linear. Dawn Sheik, a middle school math teacher with active shooter training, was among the first to move, turning to her daughters and then to the rows around her to shout at people to run, while Bishop Jeffrey Schaub reached the microphone and directed everyone out the back doors. Congregation members want the four who died named first, calling them the heroes of that day: Thelma Armstrong, 54; John Bond, 77; Craig Hayden, 72; and William "Pat" Howard, 77. Members credit those eight minutes of terror, and the reactions inside them, with saving more than 200 lives, but describe a year since spent circling guilt and second-guessing. Many said the attack forced them into the hardest questions about suffering and where God is in a tragedy, and that telling their stories has become part of how the healing continues.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: New hymn ‘Peace, Peace, Be Still’ brings hope through the Savior to face life’s storms
item.description: Sally DeFord wrote the words to the new hymn "Peace, Peace, Be Still" while recovering from hand surgery, a trial she took at the time to be a hard one. Steeper ones followed, including multiple sclerosis, a daughter's cancer diagnosis and a recent stroke, sending her back to the refuge the lyrics describe in Jesus Christ, who rules the rising storm. Writing to the Church News on his wife's behalf, Dennis DeFord noted that the turmoil in each stanza softens and resolves into the Savior's command and invitation, echoing the psalm's call to be still and know that I am God. The full account is published at TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: October 2026 general conference: How to watch, listen and follow
item.description: The 196th Semiannual General Conference of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints runs Oct. 3-4 with four sessions rather than five, the second conference held under the schedule the faith adjusted in fall 2025. Sessions start at 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. Mountain Daylight Time each day, last about two hours and originate from the Conference Center in Salt Lake City, with President Dallin H. Oaks presiding over all of them. Live coverage will run in more than 70 languages on broadcasts.ChurchofJesusChrist.org, alongside the General Conference YouTube channel in 14 languages, the Gospel Stream app in four and Gospel Library in 80. Bonneville Distribution handles satellite and broadcast carriage, including Dish Channel 9403, DirecTV channels 374 and 68 in Utah, BYUtv and KSL-TV Channel 5, while KSL NewsRadio airs the sessions on 102.7 FM and BYU Radio on SiriusXM Channel 143. In a recent letter to congregation leaders worldwide, the First Presidency framed conference as an opportunity to receive personal revelation and encouraged members to listen, study, ponder and apply the counsel given.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: B’Nai Israel Temple religious legacy lives on in Salt Lake Art Museum
item.description: The former B'nai Israel Temple at 249 S. 400 East in Salt Lake City reopened on July 24 as the Salt Lake Art Museum, its first exhibit devoted to the synagogue's own history. Utah's Jewish story traces back to Fanny Brooks, who passed through Salt Lake City with her husband in 1854 and returned a decade later to settle at Third and Main; her children attended a Latter-day Saint Sunday School until the city had a synagogue of its own. Congregation B'nai Israel formed in 1873 and built near 300 South and West Temple, then split in 1885 into a Reform congregation and Congregation Montefiore, which moved from Orthodox to Conservative practice. The 400 East building was dedicated in July 1891 and served for more than 80 years before the two congregations merged as Kol Ami and sold it in 1976, after which it became a restaurant and later an office furniture showroom and headquarters for Henriksen Butler. Tour guide Kevin Earl, who researches the city's historic churches, said the exposed trusses over the gallery and nearly all the windows are original, and that Henriksen Butler's rear addition was built to meet accessibility standards without removing the original staircases.
item.dc:creator: Joe Wirthlin

item.title: Latter-day Saints around the world embrace new Sunday schedule
item.description: The revised Sunday schedule of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints compresses gospel instruction into 25-minute lesson blocks, and the Church News has been gathering members' reactions to teaching under it. Bobure Wabol, of the Bikenibeu 2nd Ward in the Tarawa Kiribati East Stake, wrote that the tighter window pushed her to settle on a single principle for each lesson rather than work through an entire assignment. She treats that constraint as a spiritual gain rather than a limitation, measuring a meeting by whether it strengthens faith in Jesus Christ. The full account is at TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: How simple invitations led 3 Church leaders to find the gospel of Jesus Christ
item.description: Elder I. Raymond Egbo was invited to church by his sister, Elder D. Martin Goury by a friend and Elder Aroldo B. Cavalcante by a cousin — three General Authority Seventies whose paths into The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints started with someone they already knew. Their accounts anchor a set of new church videos in the "Love, Share, Invite" series, which dwells less on the invitation itself than on what came after it: each man was made to feel welcome once he actually showed up. Fuller versions of the three accounts, and the videos, are at theChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: International Pentecostal conference to bring thousands to Salt Lake City
item.description: The United Pentecostal Church International will hold its annual General Conference Tuesday through Friday at the Salt Palace Convention Center, a four-day program of preaching, teaching, worship and networking for ministers and lay leaders drawn mostly from North America. Communications director Jonathan Mohr said past conferences have brought 8,000 to 10,000 people, and stressed that attendance at sessions and exhibits is not limited to Pentecostals, calling it a chance for others to learn what the movement is about. General Superintendent Dr. David K. Bernard described the gathering as a combination of worship, denominational business and collaboration across the fellowship, which counts more than six million constituents in 203 countries. The organization picks host cities for hotel capacity and venue size rather than airport access, with recent conferences in Orlando, Long Beach and Toronto; this is Utah's seventh time hosting and its first since 2004. Exhibits open Tuesday at 5 p.m. and each subsequent morning at 9, keynote addresses run at 7 p.m. nightly, and a closed business session is set for Wednesday morning.
item.dc:creator: Joe Wirthlin

item.title: Barriers down, Temple Square expands public access ahead of general conference
item.description: The construction barriers that closed off the north edge of Temple Square for nearly seven years are gone, and The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced Friday that North Temple Street is clear from State Street to West Temple. With the gates open and new stone pathways in place around the Salt Lake Temple, visitors arriving for general conference will be able to move through the square and see its statues and grounds freely. A statue titled "Jesus Christ With Mary and Martha" has been installed, and another depicting Christ blessing children is planned, which will bring the total on the square to 12. President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, speaking at a recent media event, described the church as a global one with a universal message centered on Christ. Preparations continue for the temple open house running April 5 through Oct. 1, 2027, under the theme "Rejoice in Christ," with the next batch of tickets released Oct. 1 at 6 p.m. MDT.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Among 90,000 Latter-day Saint missionaries, some find family connections
item.description: Elder Noah Doutt of Stansbury Park, Utah, and Elder Devan Hoge of Paris, Idaho, were strangers assigned adjacent seats on their flights to the Argentina Resistencia Mission, and worked out in conversation that their fathers, Nathan Doutt and Ephraim Hoge, had overlapped in the Ohio Cincinnati Mission between 1999 and 2001. Church News presents the coincidence as a sign of God's attention to detail inside a missionary force that now tops 90,000 people across more than 500 missions. The full account is at TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Truth is an act of charity not a weapon, says Ruth Okediji, recipient of Deseret News Civic Charity Award
item.description: Harvard Law School professor Ruth Okediji received this year's Deseret News Civic Charity Award, which recognizes public figures whose faith shapes civic life and strengthens democracy. In her address at Thursday night's gala she argued that truth can either divide or heal depending on whether it is wielded as a weapon or offered as an act of recognition, and called stewardship of the capacity for truth-telling and truth-receiving a fundamental responsibility for people of faith. Okediji is a leading scholar of international intellectual property law and its bearing on economic and human development, co-directs Harvard's Berkman Klein Center, and led Nigeria's delegation in work that opened copyrighted books to blind and visually impaired readers worldwide. She arrived in New York from Nigeria at age 7, took a law degree at the University of Jos and a master's and doctorate at Harvard, and has been openly Christian on a largely secular faculty, founding the Program on Biblical Law and Christian Legal Studies and helping create the Faith & Veritas gathering in 2023. Retired federal judge Tom Griffith said Christianity has come out of the closet at Harvard since her arrival; Arthur Brooks received the inaugural award last year.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: The reason church leaders sidelined a university president
item.description: Tad Walch's ChurchBeat newsletter recounts how BYU-Hawaii president John Kauwe was placed on immediate medical leave while rectal cancer and chemotherapy were breaking down his immune system and his doctors had him in isolation. His wife, Monica, described how much he was suffering. Elder Ronald A. Rasband of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles phoned Kauwe during a three-hour infusion appointment in Honolulu, having just come from a meeting with the First Presidency, who also serve as BYU-Hawaii's board of trustees and had ordered the leave. Kauwe admitted he did not like the decision and instinctively wanted to push through the pain, which he says is precisely why the leaders acted, since he needed to be told it was acceptable to stop and heal. He now calls the intervention a beautiful example of Christlike leadership and says Rasband helped him understand kindly but firmly why he had to change.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: The cost of compromise
item.description: Mariya Manzhos uses her State of Faith newsletter column to ask whether it is possible to compromise without surrendering one's principles, noting that the word carries both a practical sense of mutual concession and a moral sense of being tainted. The question follows a Wheatley Institute symposium on rights of conscience and the Constitution that culminated in a keynote by President Dallin H. Oaks at the Washington National Cathedral. Brookings Institution senior fellow Jonathan Rauch, author of "Cross Purposes," wrote in a Deseret News column that the address marked The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints leaving the culture war and embracing what he termed Christian constitutionalism, presenting nondomination, negotiation and coalition as morally virtuous rather than merely politically useful. At the symposium, Rauch and Special Olympics chairman Tim Shriver discussed the limits of compromise, with Rauch calling it the most misunderstood concept in American civic life. He pointed to James Madison, who designed a constitutional system forcing factions into constant negotiation, treating compromise as a creative engine balancing stability with adaptation and expanding social harmony as competing parties feel heard.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: Hispanic youth have a ‘critical role’ in the Church’s future, Elder Clark G. Gilbert says in Chicago
item.description: A gathering of Hispanic young people from the United States Central Area of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints drew hundreds to the Schaumburg Illinois Stake Center outside Chicago on Sunday, Sept. 20, with a broadcast carrying it to 240 more meetinghouses around the area. Elder Clark G. Gilbert addressed the group in Spanish, framing his remarks around belonging and divine love. He told them they help shape where the church is headed, and that God and the church's prophet care for them and their families. Church News reported the meeting and has posted a fuller account at TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Put yourself in the scriptures, and ‘they will come alive to you,’ Elder Andersen teaches missionaries
item.description: Elder Neil L. Andersen of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles told missionaries at a Sept. 22 devotional at the Provo Missionary Training Center that they can hear the Savior speaking directly to them if they liken the scriptures to themselves. He read from Matthew 4:19-20, the account of Jesus calling Simon Peter and Andrew to leave their fishing nets at the Sea of Galilee. Andersen drew a parallel to missionaries who set aside education, opportunities and the comforts of home and family in order to serve. He asked whether they could see themselves in that experience, saying the scriptures apply to them and will come alive spiritually in ways they have not yet felt as they place themselves within them. Church News reported the devotional, with the full account at TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: RootsTech 2027 joins celebrations heralding the Salt Lake Temple open house
item.description: RootsTech 2027 will run March 4-6 under the theme "Celebrate!", positioning the genealogy conference as a lead-in to the Salt Lake Temple's six-month open house, whose public tours begin April 5. The three-day event will offer upward of 500 classes, interactive experiences and a virtual and in-person expo hall focused on family history technology, with programming tied to themes surrounding the historic temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Paul Nauta, senior marketing communications manager for FamilySearch, called the conference a good precursor to the temple celebration and noted it draws people worldwide both online and in person. The conference theme mirrors the open house theme, "Rejoice in Christ," though specific ties between the two will be announced later. Early bird registration is open now: free to attend online, $69 for a one-day in-person pass and $99 for three days, with prices rising closer to the event.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ general counsel urges BYU students to make this daily choice
item.description: Elder Alexander Dushku, a General Authority Seventy and general counsel of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, told BYU students at a Tuesday devotional that the time comes when each person must choose what matters most. He framed the message around Julius Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon in 49 B.C., clarifying that Caesar was no role model but had grasped the weight of an irreversible decision. Dushku urged students to cross their own Rubicon of faith and be all in for the Lord, saying now is the time to choose Christ over everything. He echoed an invitation Elder Neil L. Andersen had made to BYU students a week earlier, calling himself another witness to that message. Dushku also drew a distinction between what he called the full Christ of the Restoration and a watered-down version admired only for kindness and wisdom.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Perspective: When religion meets constitutional democracy
item.description: In this commentary, Brookings Institution senior fellow Jonathan Rauch argues that a Sept. 16 speech by President Dallin H. Oaks marks The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints stepping out of the culture war and rejecting Christian nationalism in favor of what Rauch calls Christian constitutionalism. He writes that Oaks set the church at odds with the drift among other conservative Christians toward partisanship and confrontation, urging conciliation instead, and that the speech's significance lies less in new doctrine than in its context and its pitch to a secular national audience. Rauch traces the alignment of white evangelicals with the Republican Party from the 1970s and 1980s, citing Ronald Reagan's 1980 remark to conservative pastors that he endorsed them. He contends that decades of demographic decline and cultural losses bred a politics of fear that led evangelicals to embrace Donald Trump and the MAGA movement as protectors. Rauch also points to Christian nationalism and related movements such as the Seven Mountains Mandate as the ideas supplying a take-no-prisoners view of politics.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Rauch

item.title: ‘Be moral, ethical and honest,’ Elder Rasband teaches at Salt Lake Institute
item.description: Personal integrity was the subject of a Sept. 20 devotional address by Elder Ronald A. Rasband of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles at the Salt Lake Institute of Religion, near the University of Utah. Drawing on episodes from his own life and on scriptural examples, he told students that integrity carries across marriage, business, relationships and service, and that it holds even with no one watching. His counsel to them was to be moral, ethical and honest.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Latter-day Saints among the most likely Americans to report happy family life, says major new study
item.description: A Pew Research Center survey released Tuesday found that Hindus, Jewish people and Latter-day Saints are the American religious groups most likely to describe their family lives as excellent or very good, with close to 70% of Latter-day Saints rating theirs positively. Pew drew on a larger study conducted between July 2023 and March 2024, interviewing 565 self-identified Latter-day Saints and 316 former members, with a margin of error of 6.2%. The findings portray Latter-day Saints as among the most religious adults in the country, praying and attending services more often than any other group, while also showing greater internal diversity and weaker retention. Pew noted that the softer religiosity and retention figures generally track broader national movement toward secularization. The survey covered only the United States, even though most church members live elsewhere, and it lands as the church reports record convert baptisms and missionary numbers.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Sister Yee invites Utah Valley Institute students to be the Lord’s hands in caring for those in need
item.description: Sister Kristin M. Yee, second counselor in the Relief Society general presidency, addressed a full chapel and overflow of students at the Utah Valley Institute of Religion in Orem. She told the audience they were meant to change the world through Jesus Christ and said no greater cause exists for them to take up. Yee tied that capacity to their baptismal and temple covenants and to exercising priesthood authority in their callings and assignments. The Deseret News item is a brief summary that points readers to TheChurchNews.com for the full account.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ opposes abortion measure in a second state
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has come out against a Nevada abortion ballot initiative, marking the second state where it has taken such a position, according to a letter the Deseret News authenticated. The letter went to the church's 339 Nevada congregations and was signed by General Authority Seventies Michael A. Dunn, Joaquin E. Costa and Pedro X. Larreal of the U.S. Southwest Area Presidency, who instructed local leaders to read it from the pulpit on the last two Sundays of September. A separate area presidency letter asked members in Idaho to oppose a comparable measure there. At issue in Nevada is Question 6, the Right to Abortion initiative on the Nov. 3 ballot, which would write a right to abortion into the state constitution; it already passed in 2024 with 64% of the vote and must clear a second consecutive even-year election under state law. The Nevada Catholic Conference and Catholic bishops are also campaigning against it.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Jimmer Fredette, Steve Young, 6 apostles to speak at Latter-day Saint college devotionals
item.description: An excerpt from the weekly ChurchBeat newsletter lays out the fall devotional speaker lineup at the five colleges and universities sponsored by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Steve Young, a member of both the Pro Football and College Football halls of fame, speaks at BYU-Idaho on Nov. 17, and Jimmer Fredette, who played for Team USA's 3x3 basketball team at the 2024 Olympics, speaks Nov. 10 at BYU-Hawaii. At least one apostle is scheduled at each of the five schools, with six appearing across the season. BYU-Hawaii President John “Keoni” Kauwe said this week the church has roughly 3 million college-age members, and the church heavily subsidizes tuition for the 150,000 students at its schools. It also runs a global Institute program serving 350,000 students at 2,700 locations tied to other colleges.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Kansas’ first Latter-day Saint temple opens for tours. Here are photos
item.description: Media tours of the Wichita Kansas Temple began Monday, marking the first open house for a Latter-day Saint temple in Kansas. Public tours run from Thursday, Sept. 24, through Oct. 10, free and open to all ages and faiths, with closures on Sundays and on Saturday, Oct. 3, for the church's semiannual general conference. Elder Patrick Kearon of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles will dedicate the temple on Sunday, Nov. 1. President Russell M. Nelson announced the Wichita temple in April 2022 general conference and construction started in September 2024; it will serve roughly 40,000 Latter-day Saints statewide, including more than 14,500 in the immediate region, who previously traveled to Oklahoma or Missouri. A church news release says the design draws on the area's wheat fields and sunflowers, with an interior palette of sage green, golden wheat, soft paprika and buttercream.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: A bright future for American faith? Reasons for optimism in Latter-day Saint data
item.description: The Deseret News examines why American religious decline and religious deepening appear to be happening at once, using Latter-day Saint data as a case study. The piece opens with President Dallin H. Oaks' 23-minute address at the Washington National Cathedral on the U.S. Constitution as a vehicle for peacemaking, religious freedom and unity, and the panel afterward in which Rabbi David Saperstein noted that worship attendance, belief in God and religiously grounded identity remain strong even as affiliation falls. BYU professor Justin Dyer told the paper that people less inclined toward religion now shed their religious identity more readily than in the past. The article then aggregates 10 patterns from the past decade, beginning with Church News reporting by Dave Schneider showing membership rose in 49 of 50 states over 25 years, led in percentage terms by North Dakota, Tennessee, Arkansas, Texas and North Carolina, plus the District of Columbia. California was the lone state to shrink, though it still ranks second in members behind Utah.

item.title: Church celebrates 40 years in Democratic Republic of the Congo
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is marking 40 years in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which granted the faith legal recognition in 1986 when the country was still known as Zaire. Membership has grown from a small group to about 160,000, supported by seven missions, a missionary training center, one dedicated temple and three additional temples under construction or in planning. A commemorative ceremony held in Kinshasa on Sept. 3 drew government officials, religious leaders, church leaders and members from across the country. The Africa Newsroom reported that the event also honored Congolese pioneers whose perseverance helped establish the church there.
